Seminar Title:

Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Rainfall-Driven Flood Hydrograph Prediction on the River Severn-A critical evaluation of physics-informed flood forecasting.

Seminar Type:

Departmental Seminar

Department:

Civil Engineering

Speaker Name:

Asrar Ul Haque,

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Seminar Hall, Department of Civil Engineering

Date and Time:

07 Sep 2026 10:00 AM

Contact:

Dr. Anurag Sharma

Abstract:

Physics-informed neural networks are increasingly applied to flood forecasting on the premise that embedding a governing equation within the loss function yields models that are simultaneously more accurate, more tolerant of observational noise, and more physically interpretable than purely data-driven alternatives. This study evaluates all three propositions on 132 flood events recorded on the River Severn, United Kingdom, forecasting river stage at Bewdley one day ahead from upstream gauges at Buildwas and Montford. The evaluation protocol proved more influential than any subsequent modelling decision: an unconstrained neural network assessed on the events used to train it attained a median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.9999, whereas the same network assessed on withheld events attained 0.237. The rainfall term conventionally adopted in such models assumes precipitation raises stage on the day it falls, disregarding catchment routing. Replacing this instantaneous term with a learnable distribution of rainfall over subsequent days increased withheld-event scores from 0.666 to 0.751 for single-step prediction, and from 0.107 to 0.346 when the model was advanced on its own output, against 0.679 and -0.087 for an identically configured network without the term. The recovered response peaked at a one-day lag, consistent with the propagation time obtained independently from the gauge records, and the estimated drainage rate became physically plausible (6.4 days, against 21 days). In a controlled comparison holding model family, lag order, target transform, partition and metric constant, upstream discharge raised scores by 0.187, 0.137 and 0.123 for ridge regression, gradient boosting and random forests respectively, improving 26 to 27 of 28 test events (p < 0.0001), whereas lag order alone contributed at most 0.058. The strongest forecast was obtained from ridge regression with upstream forcing, reaching 0.949 for single-step prediction and 0.932 under a chronological partition, against 0.540 for persistence. With upstream discharge available the physics term conferred no accuracy benefit (0.896 against 0.922) but substantially improved tolerance to noise, sacrificing 0.017 on an uncorrupted record while gaining 0.398 at 20% noise. These results indicate that the information supplied to a model exerts a greater influence on forecast skill than the architecture selected to process it.
